sentences.text: The Mascarene parrot measured 35 cm in length.
Its wingspan reached 211 mm, with a tail measuring between 144 and 152 mm, a culmen of 32 to 36 mm, and a tarsus of 22 to 24 mm.
This bird featured red legs and naked red skin around its eyes and nostrils.
Stuffed specimens and older descriptions indicate the body was brown and the head was bluish.
The two surviving specimens of the Mascarene parrot differ significantly in their coloration.
In 1674, Dubois described live specimens of the Mascarene parrot as "petit-gris," a color similar to the dark phase of the red squirrel.
Hume described the color of the Mascarene parrot as a dark blackish grey or brown.
The Mascarene parrot skull lacked a mandibular fenestra, had a broadly oval mandibular symphysis with a flattened lower margin, and a sharply angled downward symphysis.
Only two stuffed specimens of the Mascarene parrot exist today, located in Paris and Vienna.
The Mascarene parrot was the last endemic bird species to go extinct on Réunion.
The Mascarene parrot was first mentioned by French traveler Sieur Dubois in his 1674 travelogue of Réunion.
The Mascarene parrot was scientifically described in 1771.
The Mascarene parrot was scientifically described as Psittacus mascarinus by Carl Linnaeus in 1771.
The species name mascarinus references the Mascarene Islands, named after Portuguese discoverer Pedro Mascarenhas.
In 1834, German zoologist Carl Wilhelm Hahn published an account of a live Mascarene parrot belonging to King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria.
The IUCN Red List accepts the 1834 Hahn account as the final mention of a live Mascarene parrot.
Because several specimens were kept in captivity, the Mascarene parrot was likely not a specialized feeder.
A 1705 description by Jean Feuilley suggests that Mascarene parrots fattened themselves seasonally.
X-ray comparisons show that subfossil bones of the Mascarene parrot were intermediate in measurements between modern specimens and the stuffed ones.
The genus Mascarinus was established by Lesson in 1831.
The genus Mascarinus is classified within the parent group Psittaculini.
The IOC World Bird List emended the binomial name to M. mascarin in 2016 to align with Linnaean conventions.
The genus name Mascarinus prevailed, and when combined with the specific name mascarinus in 1891, it formed a tautonym.
A 2011 genetic study placed the Réunion Mascarene parrot among subspecies of the black parrot (Coracopsis nigra) from Madagascar and nearby islands.
The Mascarene parrot is recorded as extinct in 1834.
The Mascarene parrot was endemic to the island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean.
The last known account of wild Mascarene parrots on Réunion dates to the 1770s.
The genus Mascarinus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The date and cause of extinction are unclear; while 1834 is the latest record, it is considered dubious, suggesting extinction likely occurred before 1800 or even earlier.
Early writers incorrectly claimed the parrot was found on Madagascar, leading Lesson to propose the synonym Mascarinus madagascariensis in 1831.
The evolutionary affinities of the Mascarene parrot have been debated since the mid-19th century.
It is suggested that the removal of the skull and mandible prior to Forbes' study may have distorted the shape of the head and nostrils in his illustrations.
Hume proposed that the brown coloration of the Mascarene parrot is an artifact of aged taxidermy, but this hypothesis is debated by researchers like Joseph M. Forshaw.

The taxonomic placement of the Mascarene parrot is debated, with recent genetic studies favoring its grouping with Psittaculini parrots over vasa parrots.
